plan.topic: Tirzepatide and prediabetes: the SURMOUNT-1 3-year analysis in adults with obesity and prediabetes (randomized vs placebo, 176 weeks), with the AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 GLP-1 vs metformin study (observational, Nov 2 2026) as the news hook
plan.angle: Hook: 'A study being presented at the American Heart Association meeting this week linked GLP-1 medicines to lower type 2 diabetes risk than metformin in adults with prediabetes and obesity. It's real-world records and not yet peer-reviewed, so it shows a link, not proof.' Payoff: 'The randomized evidence is older. In SURMOUNT-1's three-year analysis, published in 2024, 1,032 adults with prediabetes and obesity or overweight were followed for 176 weeks. 1.3% on tirzepatide developed type 2 diabetes, versus 13.3% on placebo. Seventeen weeks after stopping treatment, it was 2.4% versus 13.7%.' Then: prediabetes alone isn't an approved use; the GI line; a question for your doctor ('Given my blood sugar and weight, could a GLP-1 medicine be an option, and what else lowers my diabetes risk?'); the Exp F line; 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line. Loop back to the opening question. Possible title: 'Tirzepatide and Prediabetes: Does It Lower Risk?'
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide and Prediabetes: What a 3-Year Trial Found
plan.why: The AHA prediabetes story peaks in 2–6 days and is a large, high-CPM US audience with thin creator coverage. Putting a tirzepatide-first randomized result in an obesity population behind the hook fits the 13:00 lead rule. | fact-check: Both sources check out, but the angle needs framing fixes. AHA: the newsroom release is dated Nov 2 2026, abstract MDP1524, presented at Scientific Sessions Nov 6–9 in Chicago. It's an observational EHR study of 256,492 adults with prediabetes AND obesity, comparing GLP-1 medicines as a class (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) with metformin. It found a 31% lower relative risk of type 2 diabetes. It isn't peer-reviewed yet and didn't analyse drugs one by one. So: say 'GLP-1 medicines', not tirzepatide; call it 'an abstract being presented at the AHA meeting this week, not yet peer-reviewed'; and give no absolute claim the abstract doesn't report. The '41% lower death' figure is observational, so leave it out. SURMOUNT-1 3-year (Jastreboff et al., NEJM, published online Nov 2024; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39536238/): 1,032 adults with prediabetes and obesity or overweight. At 176 weeks, 1.3% on tirzepatide vs 13.3% on placebo developed type 2 diabetes. After 17 weeks off treatment, it was 2.4% vs 13.7%. This is two-year-old data, so never call it 'new' or 'fresh'. It's the randomized backup to a fresh observational hook. Give both arms as absolute percentages, and don't use 'nearly 99% stayed diabetes-free' or the hazard ratio alone. The off-treatment rise (1.3% → 2.4%) should be said plainly. Keep 'prediabetes on its own isn't an approved use'. Don't hashtag drugs the AHA study didn't analyse individually.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide and Prediabetes: Does It Lower Risk?
script.hook_pattern: Opens on a moment viewers recognise ("Told you have prediabetes?") and names the worry. Next comes the dated news hook: an observational AHA abstract from early November 2026 that links GLP-1 medicines, compared with metformin, to lower risk. It is a link, not proof. The stronger evidence follows: the older randomized SURMOUNT-1 result, with both arms as absolute percentages, then the tirzepatide group's rise after stopping, said plainly. It ends on agency (a question for your doctor), then the safety lines, the Exp F subscribe line and the soft CTA.

factcheck.summary: The science holds up. I checked every number and description against primary sources. SURMOUNT-1 3-year analysis (Jastreboff et al., NEJM, PMID 39536238): 1,032 adults with prediabetes and obesity or overweight, 176 weeks, type 2 diabetes in 1.3% on tirzepatide (all doses) vs 13.3% on placebo (HR 0.07), and 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off treatment (HR 0.12). The script matches all of it. The AHA abstract MDP1524 is real. It was released on 2 Nov 2026 and is an observational TriNetX health-records study of 256,492 adults with prediabetes and obesity, comparing GLP-1 medicines (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) with metformin. It isn't peer-reviewed. The script calls it "a link, not proof" and uses class wording ("G-L-P-one medicines"), which is correct. "Prediabetes alone isn't an approved use" is accurate: Zepbound's indications are chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea, not diabetes prevention. Nausea is among the most common side effects. The safety lines are there: the don't-stop line, "Not personal advice", the prescriber line, the Exp F line in the second-to-last position and the standard CTA. No title is spoken. The title is answered honestly, and the randomized evidence is kept separate from the observational evidence. Only minor fixes are needed. The most important one is replacing the AHA source URL: it points to the newsroom landing page, not the release itself.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits at -13.5 dB under voice and -15 in pauses, so a small +1.2 dB nudge (gain 1.15) lifts pauses toward -14 without breaking the -12 to -15 window. Fixed several outlier cues: a near-clipping pop at 5.82s and a swoosh at 34.81s that were almost as loud as the voice, a too-loud swoosh at 48.86s, two inaudible swell/tick cues at 28.27s boosted to max, and thinned redundant stacked effects (duplicate whoosh at the 19.08s caveat beat, a duplicate swoosh at 57.57s, and a redundant second pop at 63.06s) to stay within the 3-4-per-second limit and keep the "link, not proof" and disclaimer lines calm.
